ai-what-is-ai.title: What AI really is
ai-what-is-ai.body: ## A very good guesser of words The AI chat tools you hear about (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini) are **large language models**. They learned from a huge amount of text and became very good at one thing: predicting what text should come next. That simple skill turns out to be powerful. To continue a question well, the model has to pick up grammar, facts, reasoning steps and even how code works. ## What it is good at - Explaining things in simple words, in many languages - Writing and rewriting: emails, posts, summaries, lesson notes - Writing code, and explaining code line by line - Brainstorming ideas and plans ## Where it goes wrong - It can sound sure and still be **wrong** (people call this a *hallucination*) - It may not know recent news unless it can search - It does not *know you* unless you tell it what you need > Think of AI as a fast, well-read assistant: brilliant at first drafts, but you are still the editor.

ai-prompts.title: Asking AI well (prompting)
ai-prompts.practice: Write a prompt with all 4 parts for something real in your life or work. Send it to the tutor: it will answer, then score your prompt and show how to make it stronger.
ai-prompts.body: ## The 4 parts of a good prompt 1. **Role or context**: who is asking, and why. *"I run a small pharmacy in Abuja."* 2. **Task**: exactly what you want. *"Write a WhatsApp message announcing our new opening hours."* 3. **Details and limits**: length, tone, language, what to include or avoid. *"Under 60 words, friendly, in English and Pidgin."* 4. **Format**: how you want the answer. *"Give me 3 versions as a numbered list."* ## Weak vs strong - Weak: *"write about my shop"* - Strong: *"I sell phone accessories in Lagos to students. Write 3 short Instagram captions for our back-to-school sale (20% off chargers). Fun tone, max 2 emojis each."* ## Keep the conversation going If the answer is not right, do not start again. Say what to change: *"Shorter, and mention we deliver."*

ai-check-answers.title: Checking AI answers
ai-check-answers.practice: Ask the tutor a factual question you can check (for example "What is the capital of Australia?" or a calculation). Then ask it "How sure are you, and how can I check?"
ai-check-answers.body: ## The 3-question check Before you use an AI answer for anything important, ask: 1. **Can I verify it?** Look for the fact in an official or trusted source (a government site, the company's own page, a textbook). 2. **Does it add up?** Check numbers yourself. A calculator beats a guess. 3. **Is it current?** Prices, laws and people in office change. Ask the AI where the information comes from and how recent it is. ## Ask the AI to help you check - *"How sure are you about this? What could be wrong?"* - *"Give me the sources I should check this against."* - *"Show your working step by step."* ## Never paste private things Do not paste passwords, card numbers, PINs or other people's private data into any AI chat.

ai-build-with-ai.title: Build a web page with AI
ai-build-with-ai.body: ## You describe it, AI writes the code In **Build** you type what you want, for example: > *A one-page site for "Mama Nkechi's Kitchen": menu with prices in naira, opening hours, a WhatsApp order button, warm orange colours.* The AI writes the HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and you see it running straight away. Then you keep talking to it: *"make the menu two columns"*, *"add a photo gallery"*. ## Learn while you build Every change comes with a short **what changed and why**, and you can open the **Code** tab to see and edit the code yourself. Tap **Explain** on any project to have the code explained line by line. ## Share it Press **Publish** to get a link anyone can open, and others can **remix** it to make their own version. Go to **Build** now and make your first page.

ai-at-work.title: AI at work: 10 everyday uses
ai-at-work.practice: Pick one of the 10 uses and try it with the tutor, using what you learned about good prompts.
ai-at-work.body: ## Ten things AI can do for you today 1. Turn rough notes into a clear email 2. Summarise a long document into 5 bullet points 3. Explain a hard topic for a 12-year-old 4. Draft social media posts for a week 5. Make a study timetable from your exam date 6. Write Excel formulas (*"sum column C where column A is 'Lagos'"*) 7. Practise an interview: *"Ask me 5 questions for an accountant job, one at a time"* 8. Translate and adjust tone 9. Brainstorm business names or product ideas 10. Debug code: paste the error and ask what it means ## Your turn Pick one that matters to you this week and try it with the tutor.

web-first-page.title: Your first web page
web-first-page.task: Change the page so it has a main title (h1) with your name, a paragraph about you, and a link.
web-first-page.hint: A link looks like Text people click
web-first-page.body:
## HTML is the skeleton of a page A web page is text with **tags** around it. Tags say what each part is: ```html

Big title

A paragraph of text.

Chat on WhatsApp ``` Most tags come in pairs: `

` opens, `

` closes.

web-css.title: Colours and fonts with CSS
web-css.task: Give the page a background colour, colour the h1, and make the box with class "card" have padding and rounded corners.
web-css.hint: Inside <style>: body { background: #fff7ed; }  h1 { color: #ea580c; }  .card { padding: 16px; border-radius: 12px; }
web-css.body: ## CSS is the clothing CSS chooses colours, sizes and spacing. Put it in a `<style>` tag: ```html <style> body { font-family: sans-serif; background: #fff7ed; } h1 { color: #ea580c; } .card { padding: 16px; border-radius: 12px; background: white; } </style> ``` `h1 { ... }` styles every h1. `.card { ... }` styles everything with `class="card"`.

web-layout.title: Layout with flexbox
web-layout.task: Make the three dishes sit side by side with a gap, and let them wrap on small screens.
web-layout.body: ## Put things side by side `display: flex` puts the children of a box in a row: ```css .menu { display: flex; gap: 12px; flex-wrap: wrap; } .menu > div { flex: 1; min-width: 140px; } ``` `gap` is the space between them, and `flex-wrap: wrap` lets them go to the next line on small phones.

web-js-basics.title: JavaScript: variables and functions
web-js-basics.task: Write a function called total(price, plates) that returns price × plates, and show "Total: ₦10500" for 3 plates of ₦3,500 in the paragraph with id="total".
web-js-basics.hint: function total(p, n) { return p * n }  then  document.getElementById('total').textContent = 'Total: ₦' + total(price, plates)
web-js-basics.body:
## JavaScript makes pages think ```html

``` - `const` stores a value - a **function** is a reusable recipe: give it inputs, it gives back an answer - `document.getElementById(...)` finds an element so you can change it

web-events.title: Buttons that do things
web-events.task: Make the + button add 1 and the − button take away 1 (never below 0). Show the number in #count.
web-events.body:
## Listen for clicks ```html

Plates: 0

``` `let` is a value that can change. `addEventListener('click', ...)` runs your code every time the button is clicked.

app-todo.title: A to-do list app
app-todo.task: When "Add" is clicked, add the typed task to the list (ignore empty text) and clear the box.
app-todo.hint: document.getElementById('add').addEventListener('click', () => { const t = box.value.trim(); if (!t) return; tasks.push(t); box.value = ''; show() })
app-todo.body: ## Lists of things are arrays ```js const tasks = ['Buy rice', 'Call mum'] tasks.push('Pay light bill') // add to the end tasks.length // 3 ``` To show an array on the page, clear the list and add one `<li>` per item: ```js function show() { list.innerHTML = '' for (const t of tasks) { const li = document.createElement('li') li.textContent = t list.appendChild(li) } } ```

app-save.title: Saving data in the browser
app-save.task: Write save() to store the notes array under the key "notes", and load() to return the saved array (or [] if nothing is saved).
app-save.hint: function save(notes) { storage.setItem('notes', JSON.stringify(notes)) }  function load() { return JSON.parse(storage.getItem('notes') || '[]') }
app-save.body: ## localStorage remembers things `localStorage` keeps text in the browser, even after the page is closed: ```js localStorage.setItem('name', 'Ada') localStorage.getItem('name') // 'Ada' ``` It only stores text, so turn arrays into text with JSON: ```js localStorage.setItem('tasks', JSON.stringify(tasks)) const saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('tasks') || '[]') ``` (In this lesson's sandbox, storage is pretend: it works the same way but is cleared each time.)

app-forms.title: Forms and checking input
app-forms.task: Write validPhone(text): true for a Nigerian mobile number with 11 digits starting with 0 (spaces and dashes allowed), false otherwise.
app-forms.body: ## Never trust input Before using what people type, check it: ```js function validPhone(p) { const digits = p.replace(/\D/g, '') // keep only numbers return digits.length === 11 && digits.startsWith('0') } ``` `/\D/g` is a *regular expression*: it matches every character that is not a digit.

app-calculator.title: A profit calculator
app-calculator.task: Write profit(cost, price, qty) returning the total profit, and margin(cost, price) returning the margin % to 1 decimal place.
app-calculator.body: ## Real apps do real sums A shop owner wants to know the profit on an item: - profit per item = selling price − cost price - margin % = profit ÷ selling price × 100 Round money to whole naira with `Math.round()`, and a percentage to 1 decimal with `Math.round(x * 10) / 10`.

game-canvas.title: Drawing on a canvas
game-canvas.task: Draw a green rectangle and a circle of any colour on the canvas.
game-canvas.body: ## The canvas is a drawing board ```html <canvas id="c" width="320" height="200"></canvas> <script> const ctx = document.getElementById('c').getContext('2d') ctx.fillStyle = 'orange' ctx.fillRect(20, 20, 80, 50) // x, y, width, height ctx.beginPath() ctx.arc(200, 100, 30, 0, Math.PI * 2) // a circle: x, y, radius ctx.fill() </script> ``` x goes right, y goes **down** from the top-left corner.

game-loop.title: Animation: the game loop
game-loop.task: Make the ball move to the right and come back from the left side when it leaves the canvas. Keep its position in the variable x.
game-loop.body: ## Draw, move, repeat Games redraw the screen about 60 times a second: ```js let x = 0 function frame() { ctx.clearRect(0, 0, 320, 200) // wipe ctx.fillRect(x, 80, 30, 30) // draw x = x + 2 // move if (x > 320) x = -30 // wrap around requestAnimationFrame(frame) // again next frame } frame() ```

game-keys.title: Keyboard and touch controls
game-keys.task: Move player.x 20 left or right with the arrow keys, and never let it go below 0 or above 280.
game-keys.body: ## Listen for keys ```js document.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => { if (e.key === 'ArrowLeft') player.x -= 20 if (e.key === 'ArrowRight') player.x += 20 }) ``` On phones there are no arrow keys, so add buttons that do the same thing. Keep the player inside the canvas with `Math.max` and `Math.min`.

game-dodge.title: Your first game: Dodge!
game-dodge.task: Write hit(a, b) so it returns true when the two boxes overlap, false when they do not.
game-dodge.hint: return a.x < b.x + b.w && a.x + a.w > b.x && a.y < b.y + b.h && a.y + a.h > b.y
game-dodge.body: ## Put it together A game needs: things that move, a player, a **collision** check, and a score. Two boxes touch when they overlap on both x and y: ```js function hit(a, b) { return a.x < b.x + b.w && a.x + a.w > b.x && a.y < b.y + b.h && a.y + a.h > b.y } ``` The game below is almost done: write `hit` and the game works. Use the arrow keys to dodge.

data-totals.title: Totals, averages and the best seller
data-totals.task: Write revenue(sales) for the total money, and bestSeller(sales) for the item with the most units sold.
data-totals.body: ## Data is a list of records ```js const sales = [ { item: 'Bread', qty: 4, price: 1200 }, { item: 'Milk', qty: 2, price: 1500 }, { item: 'Bread', qty: 1, price: 1200 }, ] ``` Three tools do most of the work: - `reduce` adds things up: `sales.reduce((sum, s) => sum + s.qty * s.price, 0)` - `filter` keeps some rows: `sales.filter(s => s.item === 'Bread')` - an object can count per item: `by[s.item] = (by[s.item] || 0) + s.qty`

data-chart.title: Draw a bar chart
data-chart.task: Draw one bar per month (4 bars) on the canvas, with heights that follow the sales.
data-chart.hint: months.forEach((m, i) => { const h = sales[i] / Math.max(...sales) * 150; ctx.fillStyle = "#e11d48"; ctx.fillRect(30 + i * 70, 170 - h, 40, h) })
data-chart.body: ## A picture of the numbers A bar chart is just rectangles whose height follows the value. Scale the tallest bar to fit: ```js const max = Math.max(...values) const h = value / max * 150 // 150px for the tallest ctx.fillRect(x, 170 - h, 30, h) ```
